newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq on diplomatic move for easing of sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iraq on diplomatic move for easing of sanctions.

text.p: Iraqi officials are visiting foreign countries in a bid to win support for the lifting of trade sanctions while U.N. officials overseeing Baghdad's disarmament say they note more cooperation from the Iraqi side.

Diplomats based in Baghdad said Iraq hopes to be able to remove remaining constraints on its oil sales by the end of this year, something that cannot happen until a special U.N. commission agrees that Iraq has gotten rid of its weapons of mass destruction.
Under a special oil deal with the United Nations, Iraq is now allowed to sell a limited amount of oil over a six month period to buy food and medicine for Iraqis hard hit by the embargo.
But the overall sanctions -- imposed on iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait -- remain, including a ban on free oil exports by Iraq and severe restrictions on its trade with the outside world.

Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz was in Russia early this month where he is said to have pledged full cooperation with the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) disarming Iraq under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire conditions.

One European diplomat said Aziz was given assurances by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, keen to improve ties with the allies of the former Soviet Union such as Iraq, that Moscow will do everything possible to have the ban on Iraqi oil exports removed by the end of the year.

U.N. disarmament officials in Baghdad said they recently noted a high degree of cooperation from the Iraqi side. They said U.N. weapons inspectors made spot visits to several sensitive sites in and around Baghdad that in the past Iraq had declared off limits.

Iraq last month let UNSCOM transfer more than 100 pieces of scrapped long-range missiles to the United States for analysis. Earlier it said it would not allow the commission to have them examined by Washington.
Meanwhile, Aziz, according to the Iraqi official press, was now in Brussels, trying to win the backing of Belgium and other EU countries for an end to the oil embargo.
Baghdad newspaper said Aziz's main task was to try prove to EU members that Iraq had no interest in keeping any of its banned weapons and was keen to restore its place in the international community.
EU countires, apart from Britain, are sending overtures.
Spain last month sent a senior diplomat to Baghdad to run its embassy manned in the past six years by local staff.

"Of course there are U.N. resolutions to be implemented but it will be a big mistake to igonore a country like Iraq with its oil potential and strategic position in the region," the new charge d'affaires said.
Last month Italy also sent a charge d'affaires to run its interests section working under a Hungarian flag while France has a senior diplomat running its interests section at the Romanian embassy.
"Those without permanent representation like Germany, Australia, Belgium and others, send diplomats from Amman to Baghdad every one or two months and stay for a couple of weeks," one diplomat said.
